cards.front: What happens to an object when the resultant force acting on it is not zero?
cards.back: It **accelerates** in the direction of the resultant force, so its speed, its direction, or both change. The resultant force is the single overall force after combining all forces on the object.
cards.hint: Think about what the overall force does, not each separate force.

cards.front: Which equation calculates acceleration from the change in velocity and the time taken?
cards.back: $\text{acceleration}=\frac{\text{final velocity}-\text{initial velocity}}{\text{time taken}}$, measured in **$\mathrm{m/s^2}$**. It is the change in velocity per unit of time.
cards.hint: Compare with how speed is found from distance and time.

cards.front: What does the gradient of a velocity–time graph represent?
cards.back: **Acceleration**. A horizontal line means zero acceleration, and a straight sloping line means constant acceleration.
cards.hint: Compare with what the gradient of a distance–time graph gives.

cards.front: What unit does speed have when distance is in metres and time is in seconds?
cards.hint: Work out the unit from the formula, one quantity at a time.

cards.front: A cyclist travels 150 m in 30 s. What is their average speed?
cards.hint: Start with the average speed equation and substitute the values.

cards.front: What does a steeper rising line on a distance–time graph show?
cards.back: A **greater speed**, because the gradient equals the change in distance divided by the change in time.
cards.hint: Think about what the gradient represents on this graph.

cards.front: Why is average speed not enough to describe a journey that speeds up and slows down?
cards.back: Average speed uses total distance and total time, so it **does not show** whether the object sped up or slowed down during the trip.
cards.hint: Consider what information a single total hides.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that acceleration always means speeding up?
cards.back: **Acceleration** is any change in velocity. Slowing down counts, and so does turning at constant speed, because the direction of velocity changes.
cards.hint: Think about what velocity includes beyond speed.

cards.front: How does a falling object reach a constant terminal velocity?
cards.back: 1) Weight is greater than air resistance, so it accelerates downwards. 2) Air resistance rises as speed increases. 3) The forces balance, the resultant force is zero, and the object reaches **terminal velocity**.
cards.hint: Start by asking which force is bigger when the object first falls.

cards.front: Why does a moving object keep going at constant velocity when its forces are balanced?
cards.back: The **resultant force is zero**, so there is no acceleration. The object does not need a force to keep moving; a resultant force is only needed to change its motion.
cards.hint: Think about what a resultant force of zero does to motion.

cards.front: A car's velocity rises from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. What is its acceleration?
cards.back: **$2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$**. The change in velocity is $16-4=12\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $12\div6=2$.
cards.hint: Find the change in velocity before dividing by the time.

cards.front: What does the area under a velocity–time graph give when velocity stays positive?
cards.back: The **distance travelled**. In general the area gives displacement, including direction, so areas below the time axis count as negative.
cards.hint: Compare the units of area with the units on each axis.

cards.front: Why can a distance–time line never slope downwards?
cards.back: **Total distance** cannot decrease over time, so the line can only stay level or rise.
cards.hint: Think about what distance measures as time passes.
